## DI-0301 continues: two threads about one question

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is back with the next piece of **DI-0301**, her data-integrity
self-assessment. Two things are sitting on her desk, and they turn out to be the same question
wearing two different coats.

**Thread one** picks up something module 1 left hanging. Her first test case, **DED-0458** — the
BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) donor-eligibility determination she ran through
ALCOA (attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded, original or a true copy, accurate) —
passed "original or a true copy" today, because the live BECS record is what's being examined. But
she flagged a nuance: what happens the day someone decides it's easier to just keep a printed
report instead of going back into BECS? Is that printout still the real record, or a copy standing
in for something it can't actually replace? She never answered that. She's back to answer it now.

**Thread two** is new. DI-0301 has reached Fairview, one of Lakeshore's satellite collection sites,
where donor-eligibility interviews are still conducted using a paper donor file — pen, clipboard,
a physical folder per donor. For central reporting, certain fields from that paper file — donor
ID, determination, date — get typed into BECS afterward, so Lakeshore's central systems can see
Fairview's activity alongside every other site's. Your QA asks the obvious question, and gets an
answer that worries her more than a wrong answer would have: nobody at Fairview, and nobody at
Quality, had ever actually decided which of the two — the paper file or the BECS entry — is the
**record of record**. The standard operating procedure (SOP) covering donor eligibility at
Fairview doesn't say. It was just never written down.

No citations yet. Just two open questions, both circling the same thing: when a record exists in
two forms, which form is actually the one that counts?

## Why this matters — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure both threads are circling. A record that exists in two places, with nobody
having decided which one is authoritative, isn't "extra safe because there are two copies." It's
the opposite. If the two copies ever disagree — a re-keying error, a field skipped, a timestamp
drift — nobody can say which one is wrong, because nobody decided in advance which one was ever
supposed to be right. The ambiguity itself is the failure, long before any specific field turns out
to be incorrect.

You already carry the instinct for this. In configuration management, you've almost certainly lived
the moment where a CMDB (configuration management database) says one thing about an asset — its
owner, its location, its patch level — and a spreadsheet someone built years ago for a specific
project says something else. Nobody intended for the spreadsheet to become anyone's reference, but
it did, and now two "sources of truth" exist for the same fact. The fix in ordinary IT governance is
always the same: designate the authoritative source, in writing, and treat the other one as a
convenience view at best.

Here's where the regulated world demands more. In ordinary IT, an authoritative-source disagreement
between a CMDB and a spreadsheet is a process-hygiene problem — worth cleaning up, rarely urgent on
its own. For a record a predicate rule already requires Lakeshore to keep, failing to document which
format is authoritative isn't just untidy. It means nobody can say, with evidence, whether the
record satisfies ALCOA or Part 11 (21 CFR Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures) at
all — because ALCOA's and Part 11's protections (review, retention, signature controls, audit-trail
review) only mean something once you know which artifact they're supposed to be protecting. The
ambiguity is the compliance gap. Not a future risk of one — the gap itself, today, as written.

## The rule in plain English

Three ideas untangle both of DI-0301's threads. Here they are, in order.

**First: a "predicate rule" is just the regulation that already required the record to exist, before
Part 11 ever entered the picture.** Part 11 doesn't invent new recordkeeping duties. It never tells
Lakeshore it has to start keeping a record it wasn't already required to keep. What it does is set
conditions for when an *electronic* version of a record some other regulation already demands can
count as trustworthy and legally equivalent to paper. For DED-0458, the predicate rule is 606.160
(21 CFR 606.160, Records) and 606.100 (21 CFR 606.100, Standard operating procedures) — the blood
establishment current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) sections that already require a
donor-eligibility determination to be documented, whether or not BECS exists. For the automated
equipment behind it, 211.68 (21 CFR 211.68, Automatic, mechanical, and electronic equipment) plays
the same role elsewhere in this curriculum. Part 11 rides on top of whichever predicate rule already
required the record. It never stands alone.

**Second: whether a given record counts as a "Part 11 record" at all depends on what you actually
rely on, not just what format exists.** FDA's (Food and Drug Administration's) own guidance calls
this the "narrow interpretation" of Part 11's scope, and it works like a fork in the road. If
Lakeshore *chooses* to keep a predicate-rule-required record electronically in place of paper, and
relies on that electronic version to actually perform the regulated activity (accepting or deferring
a donor, releasing a unit), Part 11 applies to it. But if Lakeshore generates a paper record, that
paper record satisfies everything the predicate rule requires, and the people doing the work rely on
the *paper* record — not an electronic copy — to do their regulated work, FDA generally doesn't
treat that as "using electronic records in lieu of paper records," and Part 11 doesn't reach the
electronic copy the same way. Reliance decides the question. Format alone doesn't.

**Third: not every record that looks the same on paper and on screen actually preserves the same
information — and that's where FDA's "static" and "dynamic" distinction comes in.** A static record
is fixed data: a paper form, a scanned image, a printout. A dynamic record is one whose format lets
the user interact with the content — change a view, reprocess the underlying data, apply a different
filter. A printout of a dynamic record isn't automatically equivalent to the dynamic record itself.
It's a single frozen snapshot of something that was built to be examined more than one way. Whether a
printout can stand in for the thing it was printed from depends on whether anything real was lost in
the printing.

Put the three together and both of DI-0301's threads answer the same way: figure out which format
is actually relied on for the regulated activity, confirm whether that format is static or dynamic,
and write the decision down. Don't leave it to whoever happens to open the file next.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |

| FDA 2003 Part 11 Scope and Application guidance, Introduction | "the 2003 Part 11 scope guidance, introduction" | Guidance tier. Defines "predicate rules" as the underlying Act, PHS Act, and FDA regulations other than Part 11 itself. | Names what 606.160 and 606.100 actually are to DED-0458 and Fairview's paper file: the rules that required the record before BECS or Part 11 entered the picture. |
| FDA 2003 Part 11 Scope and Application guidance, § III.B.1, "Narrow Interpretation of Scope" | "section three-B-one, narrow interpretation" | Guidance tier. Distinguishes choosing electronic format in place of paper (Part 11 applies) from relying on a paper record that independently satisfies the predicate rule (Part 11 doesn't reach the electronic copy the same way). | The test DI-0301 applies to both DED-0458's printout question and Fairview's paper-versus-BECS question. |
| FDA 2003 Part 11 Scope and Application guidance, § III.B.2, "Definition of Part 11 Records" | "section three-B-two" | Guidance tier. Recommends documenting, in advance, whether you rely on the electronic or paper record for each predicate-rule-required record — e.g., in an SOP. | What Fairview's SOP should have said and didn't; what DI-0301 now recommends Lakeshore write down for DED-0458 too. |
| 21 CFR 11.2 | "eleven point two" | Regulation. Lets a person use electronic records/signatures in place of paper, for records kept internally (a) or submitted to FDA (b), provided Part 11's own requirements are met. | The regulatory hook the "narrow interpretation" passage cites directly — the choice Part 11 actually governs. |

## The actual text

Start with the predicate-rule definition itself, quoted verbatim from
`sources/fda-guidance/part-11-scope-and-application-2003.md`:

> The underlying requirements set forth in the Act, PHS Act, and FDA regulations (other than part
> 11) are referred to in this guidance document as predicate rules.

"The Act" is the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act; "PHS Act" is the Public Health Service Act.
Everything else in that sentence is the point: *predicate rule* isn't a special category of
regulation. It's just FDA's own shorthand for "whatever rule already required this record," as
distinct from Part 11 itself.

Now the narrow-interpretation passage, quoted in full:

> Under the narrow interpretation of the scope of part 11, with respect to records required to be
> maintained under predicate rules or submitted to FDA, when persons choose to use records in
> electronic format in place of paper format, part 11 would apply. On the other hand, when persons
> use computers to generate paper printouts of electronic records, and those paper records meet all
> the requirements of the applicable predicate rules and persons rely on the paper records to
> perform their regulated activities, FDA would generally not consider persons to be "using
> electronic records in lieu of paper records" under §§ 11.2(a) and 11.2(b). In these instances, the
> use of computer systems in the generation of paper records would not trigger part 11.

Read that passage twice, because it's the whole module. It doesn't ask "does an electronic version
of this record exist somewhere." It asks what Lakeshore actually *relies on* to do the regulated
work. The same guidance backs that logic with a direct recommendation, quoted here from its
"Definition of Part 11 Records" section:

> We recommend that you determine, based on the predicate rules, whether specific records are part
> 11 records. We recommend that you document such decisions.

And again, more specifically, a few lines later:

> Accordingly, we recommend that, for each record required to be maintained under predicate rules,
> you determine in advance whether you plan to rely on the electronic record or paper record to
> perform regulated activities. We recommend that you document this decision (e.g., in a Standard
> Operating Procedure (SOP), or specification document).

Notice the word "in advance." FDA isn't recommending Lakeshore figure this out after an inspector
asks. It's recommending the decision get made and written down before the question ever comes up —
exactly what didn't happen at Fairview.

Here's the regulation that passage cites directly, 21 CFR 11.2, quoted in full from
`sources/cfr/11.2.md`:

> (a) For records required to be maintained but not submitted to the agency, persons may use
> electronic records in lieu of paper records or electronic signatures in lieu of traditional
> signatures, in whole or in part, provided that the requirements of this part are met.
>
> (b) For records submitted to the agency, persons may use electronic records in lieu of paper
> records or electronic signatures in lieu of traditional signatures, in whole or in part, provided
> that:
>
> (1) The requirements of this part are met; and
>
> (2) The document or parts of a document to be submitted have been identified in public docket No.
> 92S-0251 as being the type of submission the agency accepts in electronic form. This docket will
> identify specifically what types of documents or parts of documents are acceptable for submission
> in electronic form without paper records and the agency receiving unit(s) (e.g., specific center,
> office, division, branch) to which such submissions may be made. Documents to agency receiving
> unit(s) not specified in the public docket will not be considered as official if they are submitted
> in electronic form; paper forms of such documents will be considered as official and must
> accompany any electronic records. Persons are expected to consult with the intended agency
> receiving unit for details on how (e.g., method of transmission, media, file formats, and technical
> protocols) and whether to proceed with the electronic submission.

11.2(a) is the one that matters for DED-0458 and Fairview: neither record gets submitted to FDA
directly, so the relevant permission is "persons may use electronic records in lieu of paper
records... provided that the requirements of this part are met." Part 11 is the permission slip for
a *choice* — it doesn't force the choice, and it doesn't create the underlying duty to keep the
record in the first place. That duty is the predicate rule's.

Now the static/dynamic distinction, quoted verbatim from
`sources/fda-guidance/data-integrity-cgmp-qa-2018.md` (Question 1d):

> For the purposes of this guidance, static is used to indicate a fixed-data record such as a paper
> record or an electronic image, and dynamic means that the record format allows interaction between
> the user and the record content. For example, a dynamic chromatographic record may allow the user
> to change the baseline and reprocess chromatographic data so that the resulting peaks may appear
> smaller or larger. It also may allow the user to modify formulas or entries in a spreadsheet used
> to compute test results or other information such as calculated yield.

A chromatographic record is one lab technique's output; Lakeshore doesn't run that equipment, but
the pattern transfers directly. BECS's own donor-eligibility record is interactive in the same
sense: someone can query it, re-sort a donor's history, filter by a different date range, or pull up
a different view of the same underlying data. A printed report is one fixed snapshot of one of those
views, taken at one moment. That's the entire difference between static and dynamic, made concrete.

Last, the guidance's own answer on stand-alone instrument printouts, quoted in full (Question 10) —
plant this one, don't resolve it yet:

> A paper printout or static record may satisfy retention requirements if it is the original record
> or a true copy of the original record (see §§ 211.68(b), 211.188, 211.194, and 212.60). During
> data acquisition, for example, pH meters and balances may create a paper printout or static record
> as the original record. In this case, the paper printout or static record, or a true copy, must be
> retained (§ 211.180).
>
> However, electronic records from certain types of laboratory instruments—whether stand-alone or
> networked—are dynamic, and a printout or a static record does not preserve the dynamic record
> format that is part of the complete original record. For example, the spectral file created by
> FT-IR (Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy) is dynamic and can be reprocessed. However, a
> static record or printout is fixed and would not satisfy CGMP requirements to retain original
> records or true copies (§ 211.180(d)). Also, if the full spectrum is not displayed in the printout,
> contaminants may be excluded.

Hold that passage. It's doing exactly one job in this module: showing you that "is a printout good
enough" has two genuinely different right answers depending on the instrument, and that the
difference turns on whether the instrument's electronic record is static or dynamic by nature — not
on habit, or on which answer is more convenient. Lakeshore's own aging stand-alone laboratory
instrument — the one DI-0301 hasn't reached yet — raises exactly this question. Which case it looks
like, pH-meter or FT-IR, is next module's work, not this one's.

### Resolving DED-0458's nuance, now

Module 1 left this open on purpose. Here's the resolution, using this module's own framework
instead of guessing.

Apply the narrow interpretation first. Is DED-0458 a record a predicate rule requires? Yes — 606.160
requires Lakeshore to keep donor-eligibility determination records. Today, the people who perform
the regulated activity — deciding whether a donor is accepted — rely on the live BECS record, not a
printout, to do it. Under the narrow-interpretation test, that means DED-0458 is a Part 11 record:
Lakeshore chose to keep this predicate-rule-required record electronically, in place of paper, and
relies on the electronic version.

Now apply static versus dynamic. BECS's donor-eligibility record is dynamic — it's a row inside an
interactive, queryable system, open to being re-examined with different views or filters, tied to
its own audit trail and e-signature controls (the subject of last module). A printed report
generated from it is static: one frozen view, taken once. If anyone later swaps the live record for
that printout as "the" record of DED-0458, they'd be substituting a static snapshot for a dynamic
original — the same substitution FDA's Question 10 above says can't be made safely for a genuinely
dynamic record.

So the resolution: the live BECS record — not any printout generated from it — has to remain the
thing Lakeshore treats as original and record-of-record for DED-0458. That's not a new control to
build. It's a decision to make and write down, per the 2003 guidance's own recommendation: document,
in Lakeshore's SOP or specification for DED-0458's record type, that the electronic BECS record is
the relied-upon original and any printout is a convenience copy only — not a substitute, and not
itself acceptable as the retained record. The open ALCOA letter from module 1, "accurate," is still
unresolved and still someone else's job. This one closes.

### Fairview's paper file, resolved the same way

Apply the same two tests to Fairview.

**Narrow interpretation first.** What does the staff member at Fairview actually rely on, in the
moment, to decide whether to accept or defer a donor? The paper file — that's the record they
consult, write on, and act on during the interview itself. The BECS entry happens afterward, typed
in from the paper file, for central reporting. Under the narrow-interpretation test, Fairview hasn't
"chosen electronic format in place of paper" for the determination itself — it generates a paper
record that satisfies the predicate rule (606.160, 606.100) and relies on that paper record to
perform the regulated activity. By the guidance's own logic, that means Part 11 doesn't reach the
BECS re-entry the same way it would reach a record Fairview genuinely replaced paper with.

**Static versus dynamic, second.** The paper file is static by nature — ink on a form. The question
worth asking about the BECS re-entry is whether anyone at Fairview, or centrally, ever actually
*uses* that entry interactively — re-queries it, cross-checks it against another site's data,
re-sorts it — or whether it only ever gets read back exactly as typed, as a static copy of the same
facts the paper file already holds. DI-0301's honest finding: nobody had actually thought about it in
these terms. The BECS entry exists. Whether it's functioning as a dynamic, independently reliable
record or as a static mirror of the paper file was simply never decided.

**The recommendation.** As practiced today — paper relied on for the actual donor-eligibility
decision, BECS entry made afterward purely for central visibility — the paper file is Fairview's
defensible record of record, and the BECS entry is a reporting copy. That's a workable answer, but
only if Lakeshore does what the 2003 guidance recommends and actually writes it down: an SOP
statement naming the paper file as record-of-record for Fairview's donor-eligibility determination,
with the BECS entry documented explicitly as a derived reporting copy, not an independent original.
Once that's written down, the protections this course has already built — ALCOA (module 1), audit
trail review and signature controls (module 2) — apply in full to the paper file: it's the one that
needs the retention, the controlled-document handling, the review attention appropriate to being the
real record. The BECS copy still matters — a timing or accuracy gap in it could let a stale donor
status reach another site before the cumulative record catches up, which is exactly the shape of
problem this course picks up in full in module 6 — but it matters as a reporting feed, not as the
thing ALCOA and Part 11 are protecting.

One honest flag, for the choice that was logged: this module uses **Fairview** as the site still
running a paper donor file, by the drafter's own choice, consistent with (and not contradicting)
Fairview's and Brookfield's prior light appearances elsewhere in this curriculum.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor
wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore has a predicate-rule policy. They'd ask for one specific thing: proof
that Lakeshore knows, in writing, which format of each record it actually relies on.

**For DED-0458 and records like it:** a specification or SOP line naming the live BECS record as the
relied-upon original, not an assumption that "it's in BECS, so it's fine." A bad answer sounds like
"we have both the system record and a printout, so we're covered." A good answer names one of them
as authoritative and explains why the other is a convenience copy only.

**For Fairview's donor file:** the same thing, in the other direction — an SOP statement that the
paper file is the record of record, with the BECS entry named explicitly as a reporting copy. A bad
answer sounds like "we keep both, so nothing's really at risk." A good answer can point to the line
in the SOP that settles it, and show the paper file getting exactly the handling (retention, review,
protection from alteration) a record of record requires.

**For the choice itself:** evidence the decision was made *in advance*, not reconstructed after
DI-0301 asked the question. An inspector who senses the answer was invented on the spot, to satisfy
the question being asked, will probe harder — and should.

## Common traps

**"If a record exists on paper, Part 11 never applies, full stop."** Not quite. Part 11's reach
depends on reliance, not on whether paper exists somewhere. If Lakeshore relied on an electronic
record to perform the regulated activity and only generated a paper printout afterward for
convenience, the narrow-interpretation passage above says the *electronic* record is still the one
that counts — the paper copy existing doesn't retroactively exempt it. DED-0458 is the proof: BECS
is what's relied on, so BECS is the Part 11 record, printout or no printout.

**"Keeping a record in two formats is safer than keeping it in one."** DI-0301's Fairview finding
refutes this directly. Two formats with no documented decision about which one is authoritative
isn't redundancy — it's ambiguity waiting for the two copies to disagree. The fix isn't picking a
format at random. It's documenting, per the 2003 guidance's own recommendation, which one Lakeshore
actually relies on — and then making sure that one, specifically, gets the protection a real record
of record requires.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask, for any record your team touches, "which format do we actually rely on to do the regulated
  work?"** Not which format exists — which one people would actually act on if the two ever
  disagreed. That answer is the Part 11 record, regardless of what else happens to exist alongside
  it.
- **Treat "we keep it in both formats" as an incomplete answer, not a reassuring one**, until someone
  can show you the SOP line naming which one is authoritative. Fairview's gap wasn't that two formats
  existed — it's that nobody had ever written down which one mattered.
- **When a system is interactive — queryable, filterable, re-sortable — ask whether anyone has ever
  swapped a printout in for it as "the" record.** That substitution is exactly where a dynamic
  record quietly turns into a static one without anyone deciding it should.
- **Push your QA to document the reliance decision in advance, not after an inspector asks.** FDA's
  own guidance recommends this explicitly. A decision made under inspection pressure looks like what
  it is.
- **Remember predicate rules are what actually reaches a record — Part 11 is the layer on top.** If
  someone tells you "Part 11 doesn't apply here, so we're fine," ask what predicate rule still
  governs that record regardless. There's almost always one underneath.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Lakeshore's shipping desk keeps a paper temperature log, required by 21 CFR 600.15, that's physically checked before any shipment is released. For her own convenience, a supervisor also types up a spreadsheet summarizing each day's logged temperatures, used only to build a monthly chart for a staff meeting — nobody consults it to decide whether to release a shipment. Is that spreadsheet a "Part 11 record"?

No — and this is a genuine application of the narrow-interpretation test, not a simple yes/no
recall. The predicate rule (21 CFR 600.15) requires the temperature record to exist; the paper log
is what satisfies that requirement and what shipping staff actually rely on to release product. The
spreadsheet is a separate, derivative document — never relied on to perform the regulated activity,
and not itself required to be maintained under the predicate rule. Under the guidance's own test,
Part 11 reaches records required under predicate rules that are relied on in electronic format in
place of paper. This spreadsheet is neither the required record nor the one relied on. It's a
convenience copy, and FDA's narrow interpretation says the use of a computer to generate it doesn't
trigger Part 11.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Someone on your team says, "A predicate rule is a special, stricter category of FDA regulation — stricter than an ordinary CFR section." Accurate?

No, and this is worth correcting precisely. A predicate rule isn't a special or stricter category of
anything. It's FDA's own shorthand — defined in its 2003 Part 11 guidance — for whatever
regulation (211.68, 606.160, 606.100, or any other section of the Act, the PHS Act, or FDA's
regulations) already required a record to exist, as distinct from Part 11 itself. 606.160 is a
predicate rule the moment Part 11 is the thing being discussed; it's an entirely ordinary CGMP
regulation the rest of the time. Calling something "a predicate rule" doesn't change what it
requires — it just names its relationship to Part 11 in a given conversation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: DI-0301 finds that nobody at Fairview had ever decided whether the paper donor file or the BECS re-entry is the record of record. Is that finding itself a Part 11 violation?

Not exactly — and the distinction matters. Nothing in Part 11 or its predicate rules was
necessarily being violated in substance: the paper file, as actually used, likely does satisfy
606.160's and 606.100's requirements. The real finding is a documentation gap against FDA's own
*recommendation* (guidance tier, "should" language) to decide and document, in advance, which format
is relied on for each predicate-rule-required record. An undocumented decision isn't automatically a
regulation violated — it's a recommendation not yet followed, which is exactly the kind of gap a
self-assessment should catch and fix before it hardens into something worse, like the two copies
actually disagreeing with nobody positioned to say which one is right.
:::

## Where this goes next

DI-0301 now has a real answer for both of its open threads: DED-0458's live BECS record stays the
documented original, and Fairview's paper file is the documented record of record, with its BECS
entry named as a reporting copy. One question stays open on purpose — whether Lakeshore's own aging
stand-alone laboratory instrument behaves more like FDA's pH-meter example or its FT-IR example.
That's `legacy-systems-and-part-11-gaps`'s whole job next: apply FDA's own four-part legacy-system
test to that specific instrument, and answer, for Lakeshore's own equipment, the question this
module only planted.
